1:
The heading is disputed at every word. John Gill reports the old identification of Agur with Solomon, the name being read as a gatherer of wisdom who delivered it out to others; but he judges it does not fit the person whose words these are. Charles Ellicott is blunter: Jewish interpreters have seen Solomon here apparently without a shadow of reason, and the sayings probably belong to some unknown sage thought not unworthy of joining the wise King of Israel—foreign wisdom stood high then, and the book of Job is itself probably Arabian. On the word rendered the prophecy he presses a difficulty: it regularly means the message a prophet bore to his hearers, often of gloomy import, and suits neither this chapter nor the words of King Lemuel; standing alone unqualified, it is very singular. Hence the proposal to read Agur the son of Jakeh the Massan, a descendant of the Massa named among the sons of Ishmael, putting his home in North Arabia and Lemuel over that tribe. Adam Clarke reaches the same verdict from the other end: the following verses suit no part of Solomon’s life, so the chapter must be an appendix to the preceding collection, like the part gathered by the men of Hezekiah; and the mysteries found here by those who sought nothing else are hazarded and precarious. John Wesley adds that prophecy here means prophetical instruction, since prophets were preachers as well as foretellers, so their sermons no less than their predictions are called prophecies.

Clarke takes Ithiel and Ucal for real persons otherwise unknown, scholars of a teacher who delivered to them what he had by inspiration; Wesley calls them friends who desired instruction. Matthew Henry allows both readings. They may be pupils who wrote what he dictated, as Baruch wrote from the mouth of Jeremiah, and so preserved and could attest it, being two witnesses; or they may be the subject of the discourse, since one name signifies God with me and the other the Mighty One, upon whom help is laid for us—which is why many apply the verse to the Messiah. Henry also reports, without adopting, the view that Agur is not a name but a character, a collector who composed nothing but made abstracts of others. Keil and Delitzsch record the same tradition allegorising Agur as Solomon, who took the law given to the king and then set it aside.

The confession that follows is read by all as self-abasement. Gill has Agur thinking himself brutish not merely among the rest but more than any, rendering it a brute am I rather than a man. Ellicott sharpens it to rather than that I can be called a man formed in the image of God. Clarke uses the verse as evidence: the wisest of men could not have said he was more brutish than any and lacked the understanding of a man, but Agur might have said it with strict propriety, for very probably he was a rustic without education or human help, as Amos was, and all he knew now was by inspiration. Wesley hears a modest apprehension of his ignorance. Keil and Delitzsch take the next verse to say he went into no school of wisdom, so that in his wrestling after knowledge he could attain nothing, the conditions being wanting; he cannot adjudge to himself the knowledge of the all-holy God, which is the kernel and star of true wisdom. Clarke notes that the Greek version turns the clause the other way, making God the teacher. Ellicott takes the holy for the Holy One; Wesley understands the holy prophets and denies Agur had such inspiration as prophets strictly so called received. Henry gathers the point: before confessing his faith he confesses his folly, for we must go out of ourselves before we go into Christ, and the wisest man is he who knows his own ignorance.
4:
The questions that follow measure that ignorance. Charles Ellicott says they bring out the nothingness of man against the might of the Creator, in the manner of the divine speeches in Job; the waters bound in a garment he takes for clouds stretched as a curtain to keep the rain from falling. On the name he answers that we may call him self-existing, powerful, strong, merciful, gracious, but no words describe him adequately, for he has revealed himself only partially. John Wesley puts it as a challenge: what mere man? none at all; no one can know and teach these things unless he has been in heaven and sent down thence for that end; if you think any man can, produce his name, or if dead the name of his posterity. John Gill works through the candidates—Enoch was taken up before this time and Elijah probably after, but neither returned to inform mortals; Paul was caught up and came back, but what he heard was not lawful to utter—and concludes that none but Christ did this, who lay in the bosom of the Father, descended not by local motion but by assumption of nature, and ascended above all heavens. Adam Clarke reads it as saying the science of salvation is no object of study but a pure gift of God, and that Agur disclaims not the plain law common to all Israel but the sublime knowledge of God’s designs and secrets; to acquire that by one’s own strength is as hard as collecting the winds in one’s fists.

The last clause draws Clarke into a caution he cares about. He records that many refer the son’s name to the first and second persons of the Trinity, and that the versions differ here. He grants the doctrine is true, sublimely true, but asks who would rest its proof on such a text; a lover of truth should be choice in his selections, quoting nothing unclear and advancing nothing that does not tell. When we must spend a world of critical labour to establish the sense of a text we allege, we are going the wrong way to work; injudicious defenders, he ends, may be ranked among the enemies of the truth they defend.

The turn to the written word is where they converge. Gill takes every word for the whole of Scripture, purified like silver, free from falsehood since it comes from the God of truth, its promises made without dissimulation and its doctrines free of human invention. Clarke keeps the metal figure: whatever trials it meets it is like gold, bearing the fire and coming out with the same lustre, purity and weight; he notes manuscripts reading a shield to every one of them that trust. Ellicott glosses pure as tested and proved in the furnace of experience. Keil and Delitzsch supply the logic: the more limited a man is in the knowledge of God that comes by the light of nature, the more thankful he must be that God has revealed himself in history, and the more firmly he must hold fast by the pure word. On the prohibition, Clarke argues you can no more increase those words by addition than gold by adding another metal, adding and diminishing in the phrase of Scripture being to do what it forbids or leave undone what it commands; the reproof threatened is the fire showing the addition to be reprobate silver. Gill applies it against those who set an oral tradition or a church’s determinations beside the written word, and against enthusiasts who rank dreams and visions with it, holding that word alone the sufficient rule; Clarke presses the same charge against a church that canonised further writings. Ellicott renders the threat convict thee of thy falsehood, and Wesley concludes: expect the full knowledge of divine mysteries neither from me nor from any man, but from the word of God.
7:
The prayer is short by design. John Gill observes that the requests are not many and the words few: Agur made no long prayers, nor expected to be heard for much speaking. Matthew Henry takes the preface as method—consider what we need before we pray, so that we are not seeking our petition when we should be presenting it—and reads before I die as a rule for all praying: we should think of dying and pray accordingly, for if a man be not sanctified before he dies the work will not be done after, there being none of this wisdom or working in the grave. Adam Clarke takes the clause more narrowly, as wishing the answer now, so that he may live the rest of his life in the state described; Charles Ellicott glosses it while life lasts, and notes the numerical proverbs begin here.

On the first request the voices split over how wide the vanity is. Gill takes it of sin in general, which promises pleasure, profit, liberty and impunity and gives none, and asks that vain thoughts, words and actions be removed from mind, mouth and life, with the errors and false doctrines that are lies in hypocrisy. John Wesley keeps to vanity of heart and life and deceit in words and carriage; Ellicott has falsehood towards God or man; Henry hears a prayer of the same import as lead us not into temptation. Clarke goes further. The first word covers all false shows of happiness, the second all words of deception, promises which when due are like bad bills, dishonoured because the drawer is forged or insolvent—but he is satisfied from the original that Agur prays against idolatry, since the one word is elsewhere used for an idol and the other for what fails and deceives, apt enough for the promises of false gods. So read, the prayer asks preservation from idolatry and confidence in no words but God’s, which never fail them that trust in him.

The second request is for a middle state, and Henry is careful what it does not mean. Agur does not prescribe to God, nor pray against poverty or riches as evil in themselves, since either by grace may be sanctified and made a means of good; he expresses the value wise and good men have for a middle condition, and a holy jealousy of himself, that he could not keep his ground against either extreme. The bread of his allowance Henry takes as what God thinks fit to allow, or what suits a man’s rank, since as is the man so is his competency; Ellicott renders it bread of my portion, apportioned as suitable by the heavenly Father, comparing the daily bread of the Lord’s prayer; Wesley calls it moderate and suitable to natural necessities and to the condition of life God has placed him in. Clarke finds a figure from hunting—give me as prey my statute allowance of bread—the petitioner asking to be directed each day to a sufficient portion, as a hunter prays for good speed. On fulness, Gill says the rich are tempted to deny not God’s being but his providence, ascribing what they have to their own industry and supposing they can live without him; Wesley calls trusting to riches itself a denial of God, joined with unthankfulness for his mercies. Ellicott notes that pride and fulness of bread were among the sins that destroyed Sodom, and renders the other danger literally as handling the name roughly, particularly in finding fault with providence. Clarke sets the dangers side by side: want may breed a covetous spirit that distrusts its Maker and takes a neighbour’s property, then catches at the name of God to pass for innocent; plenty may breed a luxury pampering the flesh and starving the soul. Wesley adds that false oaths serve to vindicate oneself when suspected, as poor men frequently do.
10:
The warning about a servant protects the weaker party. Matthew Henry makes it a caution not to abuse other men’s servants any more than our own: the servant’s poor condition makes him an object of pity, so it is barbarous to add affliction to the afflicted, and it argues a sordid disposition to smite anybody secretly with the scourge of the tongue, especially one who is no match for us and whom we should protect if his master be severe. There is injury to the accuser too, since the man provoked may curse him, blemish his reputation, or appeal to God, the protector of oppressed innocency. John Gill presses the point practically—not rashly, not for trifles, only where the master’s business is sadly neglected; the word means to abuse with the tongue, and since masters are apt to be severe, little matters should be hidden from them rather than aggravated, and falsehoods never told. He recalls the informer who accused a fugitive to a jealous king, and the charges laid against the disciples before their Master. Charles Ellicott notes the man is a slave, whose hard life is made more intolerable, and that the guilt incurred is guilt before God. Adam Clarke adds the blunt rule not to meddle with other men’s servants. John Wesley alone marks the limit: without sufficient cause, for otherwise this may sometimes be a duty. Keil and Delitzsch reject two proposed renderings—that one should not entice a servant to slander his master, or make him tattle—holding the word means to calumniate, as later usage attests.

On the four generations the question is what is being said about them. Ellicott observes that the words there is are not in the Hebrew, leaving in doubt what the predicate of these four evil generations is, whether Agur describes the men of his own time or says that such are unbearable; the same characters, he adds, appear in the description of men of the last days. Keil and Delitzsch supply the form: this is a priamel, in which a series of subjects is followed by one briefly expressed predicate as the epigrammatic point applicable to all together—which is precisely what is missing here. Clarke numbers four grand evils of that time: ill-treatment of parents, self-righteousness, insolent pride, and greedy oppression of the poor. Henry, who calls such men in every age monsters of ingratitude, extends the first class to those who, not having arrived at cursing, still do not bless, cannot give their parents a good word, and will not pray for them.

The middle two generations draw the closest reading. Gill notes that the pure are pure neither in the eyes of God, who sees the heart, nor in other men’s, but only in their own conceit, never opened to the plague of their own hearts, the spirituality of the law, or the insufficiency of their righteousness. Henry has them swept and garnished but not washed, thinking themselves not only righteous but rich and increased with goods. Wesley puts it shortest: they imagine themselves religious while living in a course of wickedness. On the lofty eyes Gill distinguishes three scorns—the rich despising poor neighbours, the learned puffed up against the unlettered, the self-righteous saying stand by thyself, I am holier than thou—and cites the observation that pride is bred in the heart but hangs in the eyebrows, whence the proud are called supercilious. Henry hears amazement at intolerable insolence, men strutting like the peacock and thinking they make themselves illustrious when really they make themselves ridiculous. Of the last generation Gill says only that their teeth are sharp as the swords of beasts of prey; Wesley names them extortioners and cruel oppressors; Henry observes that God has so ordered it that the poor shall never cease out of the land, yet there are those who, hating to relieve them, would if they could abolish them from the earth.
15:
The leech supplies the emblem, and the voices differ over her daughters. Charles Ellicott observes that the word crying is not in the Hebrew: the creature is the emblem of insatiable greed, and if it could speak its daughters—the words it would utter—would be give, give, introducing the quartette of insatiable things that follows. John Wesley adds that nothing is commoner than to call persons the daughters of those whose examples they imitate, and notes that the writer begins with two and proceeds to three and four. John Gill canvasses the naturalists: some take the daughters for the forks of its tongue, which later inquirers find it has not, since it sucks with its three teeth or by compressing its mouth, and will not let go until filled; he judges it best to understand any that resemble it. Adam Clarke reports the moralised reading in which the leech is covetousness and her daughters avarice and ambition, and quotes a Roman poet likening a bad versifier who fastens on a listener to a leech that quits not its hold till gorged. He then offers his own conjecture, preferring it to all: the word occurs nowhere else in the Bible and may, like the other names here, be a woman’s proper name, her two daughters notorious. He notes too that the Greek version joins the two verses and gives her three daughters.

Matthew Henry reads the figure back into the generation just described. The temper that devours the poor is cruelty joined to covetousness, the two genuine offspring that cry give more blood, give more money; the bloody are still blood-thirsty, and those that love silver are never satisfied with it, for those are never rich that are always coveting. He takes the four in order—the grave, which swallows all and returns none; the barren womb, impatient of its affliction; the parched ground, which soaks in abundant rain and soon wants more; and the fire, which having consumed abundance of fuel still devours whatever is thrown in. Gill dwells on the first: the grave is the house appointed for all living, and though multitudes have been put into it, it is not full but waits for more, nor will its mouth be shut till the last enemy is destroyed—an emblem of the covetous man, who enlarges his desire as the grave and is never satisfied.

The threat against the mocking eye is its counterpart. Keil and Delitzsch note that an eye is named rather than eyes because the duality of the organ falls back before the unity of the mental activity it serves; as haughtiness revealed itself in the eyes earlier, so the eye is the mirror of humble subordination, and of the scorn that refuses reverence to father and mother. Henry connects it to the first generation and widens the offence: not only those who curse in heat and passion belong to it, but those who mock with a scornful eye, looking with disdain on a parent’s infirmities or looking sour when instructed, for God takes notice with what eye children look upon their parents and will reckon for the leering look as well as the bad language. Their doom is to be set up as monuments of vengeance, hanged as it were in chains for the birds to pick out the very eyes that looked so scornfully; if men do not punish undutiful children, God will. Clarke identifies the ravens of the valley as those that frequent places where carcasses are found, and says the mother eagle scoops out such an eye to feed her young; many disobedient to parents, he adds, have come to an untimely end and become prey to ravenous birds. Ellicott is briefer—the rebellious son shall die a grievous death, and the propensity of ravens to attack the eyes is well known—while Wesley extends it to whoever derides a parent, though but with a look.
18:
The list is built to arrive somewhere. Keil and Delitzsch point out that the new numerical proverb begins with the eagle just named, and that the turning-point lies in the fourth: the first three expressions have no object in themselves and gravitate towards the last, serving as foil to it. Charles Ellicott finds the thread elsewhere—the wonder in Agur’s eyes seems to be that none of the four leaves any trace behind. John Gill takes the opening plainly, of things above his reach, which he could not find out nor sufficiently admire, and says the bird is named because it flies swiftest and soars highest, leaving no track that can be pointed to. Matthew Henry works through the three as comparisons illustrating the fourth. The eagle’s way cannot be discovered by footstep or scent, as a beast’s may upon the ground, nor can we account for the swiftness that carries her beyond our ken. A serpent’s way in sand may be found by the track, but not upon hard rock, and no one can describe how a creature without feet gets so quickly to the top. A ship leaves no mark, and is sometimes so tossed that one wonders how it lives at sea and gains its point. The kingdom of nature, he concludes, is full of marvels past finding out.

The fourth is of another kind. Henry calls it a mystery of iniquity, more unaccountable than these, belonging to that deceitfulness of the heart which none can know, and divides it in two: the arts by which a seducer wins consent, the protestations of love, the promises of marriage, the assurances of secrecy by which many an unwary person is brought to sell honour and peace and soul to a traitor; and the arts by which an adulteress conceals what she has done, disguised so closely that discovering her is as impossible as tracking an eagle in the air. The more artfully the temptation is managed, he adds, the more resolute a pure heart ought to be against it. Adam Clarke borrows a reading that ties the two verses together by their connecting particle, making the whole a comparison: she seeks her victim as the eagle takes flight to spy out prey; she uses blandishment as the serpent employs its windings over rock; she pursues a course exposed to danger as a ship at sea; and she exercises all her sagacity to prevent discovery—conduct marked throughout by specious dissimulation.

Clarke also reports a textual doubt here. Several manuscripts and the ancient versions read in his youth rather than with a maid, a reading he thinks defensible, since the way of a man in his youth holds too many intricacies for human wisdom to explore, and only he who searches the heart knows its corrupt principles. If the received reading is kept and referred to a suspected loss of chastity, Clarke observes that the signs relied on are so equivocal as to be unascertainable, and declines to carry the matter further. On the woman’s denial the voices are brief and agreed. Gill says her way is as unknown as the one just named, since she uses so many artful methods that though she lives in adultery it is carried on so secretly that she is not easily discovered. John Wesley has her eating the bread of deceit secretly. Ellicott puts the logic of the denial in a sentence: as there is no proof of her guilt, she flatly denies it. Henry distinguishes the denial made to the world, where works of darkness are industriously kept from the light, from the denial made to her own conscience, if she have any left, where the wickedness is not owned as wickedness at all but passed off as an innocent entertainment; and he warns that multitudes ruin their souls in just this way, by calling evil good and out-facing their convictions with self-justification.
21:
The fourth numerical saying turns from wonder to grievance. John Gill reads the disquiet of the earth as the uneasiness of its inhabitants, and John Wesley calls the four intolerable in human societies. Adam Clarke treats it as another enigma and lists them: a slave who becomes ruler, an overfed fool, an ill-tempered woman set over a household, and a serving maid to whom the rule of the house has fallen. His comment on the first is that such a man, coming to bear rule, is an unprincipled tyrant; on the second, that the intellectually weak man who has everything at his command has manners none can bear, and is insupportable to everyone else if he is a favourite with his master; on the third, that a woman of ill temper once embarrassed with domestic cares is beyond bearing; and on the fourth, that a maid raised over a family, whether by the death of the mistress or the sin of the husband, becomes insolent and hateful to all.

The others fill in why each case is hard. Gill explains the first from want of training: the man is unfit through his education, having never learned the arts and maxims of government; his disposition is servile, so that as he was used when a servant he will use others; his poverty tempts him to oppressive methods of growing rich; and being raised from a low estate he is the more imperious and haughty. Gill also carries the figure over to ecclesiastical power, applying it to a ruler who styles himself the servant of servants and yet deposes kings and disposes of their kingdoms at pleasure. Wesley says much the same more briefly—commonly ignorant and therefore committing many errors, poor and therefore insatiable, proud and imperious, and usually injurious and cruel—and takes the second case to be a conceited fool who has come to abound in wealth. Charles Ellicott supplies the setting: the mischief done by favourites at court, who often began life as slaves, was proverbial; and of the fool he observes that only while he has to work hard for his living will he behave himself decently, since a little money is soon wasted in idleness and self-indulgence. On the third and fourth cases Gill takes odious to mean not deformity of body so much as the ill qualities of mind which a woman conceals while single and hides no longer once married; Wesley reads her as proud and perverse, displaying afterwards the humours she had kept back, and says of the heiress that the great and sudden change transports her beside herself. Ellicott gives both a motive rather than a temper—she pays off with interest the slights she formerly had to endure from her married friends, while the servant raised to inherit is nervously anxious to preserve her newly acquired dignity. Matthew Henry sums the four as men of low origin and base spirit who become tyrants on getting authority, foolish and violent men indulging in excesses, a woman of contentious spirit, and a servant who has obtained undue influence; and he turns the list into a warning rather than a complaint, that those whom Providence has advanced from low beginnings should carefully watch against the sin which most easily besets them.
24:
Matthew Henry reads the list as a counterweight to the last: after four things that seem great and are contemptible come four that are little and yet admirable, great in miniature. He draws four lessons—not to value persons for bulk or strength but by their wisdom and application to business; to admire the Creator as much in an ant as in an elephant; to blame ourselves, who act less for our own interest than the meanest creatures do for theirs; and not to despise the weak things of the world, since those of small account may be very wise for their souls. The margin has them made wise by the special instinct of nature; all who are wise to salvation, he adds, are made so by grace.

John Gill asks what is weaker than an ant, a multitude of which may be destroyed with one foot; one sort is so small that a hundred will not outweigh a barley corn. They are called a people because they associate in great numbers, as Scripture elsewhere speaks, and as the old poets call bees a nation. Adam Clarke adds that they store food in summer, not for winter, since they sleep through it, but for autumn and spring, and that they have their own houses, towns and roads. Henry adds that when the ravening lions suffer hunger, the laborious ants have plenty. The second creature is disputed. Charles Ellicott says flatly that coney is a mistake: the animal is the size of a rabbit but has nails instead of claws and weak teeth, and its Hebrew name signifies a hider, from its living in clefts of the rocks. Clarke agrees it is not the rabbit but a creature very like it which never burrows and dwells in holes of rocks. Gill reports the objection that rabbits burrow in sandy ground, so that many prefer the mountain mouse. Henry takes the moral whichever it is: feebleness drives them to natural fortifications, and our own weakness should drive us to him that is a rock higher than we.

The locusts are praised for order without a ruler. Keil and Delitzsch observe that guidance is not wanting though a king is: by the power and foresight of one sovereign will they march out as a body, dividing into companies ranged in order, as another prophet pictures them climbing walls like men of war, each on his appointed way and never changing his path; an ancient writer says he saw them fly as if at one command. Gill notes how devouring and how numerous they are, moving in large bodies with great regularity, which shows their wisdom by instinct; John Wesley says only that the bands are companies in exact order. Henry calls them God’s great army, mustered when he pleases, and draws the lesson that weakness should keep us together. The last creature is disputed like the second. Ellicott thinks a lizard rather than a spider is meant, and since each first line here expresses weakness prefers the rendering that one may catch it by hand and yet find it in palaces. Keil and Delitzsch record that the spelling of the word wavers in the editions and manuscripts, so that what beast is meant remains a question. Gill and Henry keep the spider and admire the workmanship: she frames her web with such exactness as if she understood mathematics and architecture, spinning from her own bowels with a fineness no art can come near. Wesley notes that her legs are called hands because they serve the same use, and that she is found in palaces as well as cottages. Henry ends where the verse does: Providence keeps up creatures which every man’s hand seeks to destroy, and those who take hold of their business with their hands shall come to kings’ palaces, for if one well-spun web be swept away it is but making another.
29:
The last numbered saying praises bearing rather than wisdom. Keil and Delitzsch mark it as another proverb built on three and one, and render the four as stately walkers: the lion, the hero among beasts, that turns back before nothing; the swift-loined; the goat; and a king with whom is the calling out of the host. The word used here for the lion, they note, is found in only one other place. John Gill takes the opening phrase of movement made with constancy and stateliness and without fear, and has the lion walking with great majesty, very slowly, step by step, the left foot first, shaking its shoulders as it goes, as the old naturalist described it. Adam Clarke says nothing can be more majestic than that walk, deliberate, equal, firm, and becoming the king of the forest. Matthew Henry makes the pre-eminence a warning: among beasts strength gives the first place, but it is a pity it should do so among men, whose honour is their wisdom and not their force. The lion turns not away nor alters his pace for any pursuer, knowing he is too hard for them, and herein the righteous are bold as a lion, turning not from duty for any difficulty.

The second creature nobody can identify. Gill canvasses the attempts and finds no agreement: one renders it greyhound, another owns he does not know what is meant, a third says only that it is a living creature, and others propose the bee, the eagle, the leopard and the starling. All the text says, he observes, is something girt about the loins, which some apply to a hunting dog, thin and as it were bound there, and others to the leopard. Charles Ellicott lists the horse, the zebra and the cock among the suggestions, concluding only that the received rendering is as probable as any. Clarke prefers the greyhound, remarkably fine and fleet in the East, and says scarcely anything can go with greater fleetness than one in full chase with its prey in view, seeming to swim over the earth. Henry accepts either that or the horse of the margin, which he thinks should not be omitted among creatures comely in going, especially when dressed in its harness.

On the third and fourth the voices agree more. John Wesley describes the goat marching at the head of the flock gravely, conducting them with courage and ready to fight for them against beasts or men; Clarke notes the state such an animal assumes before the flock, though some suppose the ram; Henry finds the comeliness precisely in going first, as it is a Christian’s comeliness to go first in a good work and lead others in the right way. Of the king, Ellicott says he marches with resistless force, trampling his conquered foes, but records the alternative, a king with whom is his people; Wesley takes that reading outright, of a king who has the hearts and hands of his people going with him. Clarke reads the clause of a king whose court, counsels and troops are so united to him as to render all hope of conspiracy vain—then adds that the Hebrew makes but two words, and raises the doubt whether this may not be another proper name, King Alkum, since the chapter abounds in such names. To the objection that we know nothing of such a king, he answers that we know nothing of Agur, Ithiel or Ucal either, and that this may have been some chieftain remembered for his good fortune; divide the word in two and the usual sense returns. Henry ends by turning all four into instruction—courage from the lion, despatch from the second, care of those under our charge from the goat, gravity in governing from the king—and adds that if there is no rising up against an earthly prince, woe to him that strives with his Maker.
32:
The closing counsel is about silence. John Gill takes the lifting up in three senses: rising against a king by speaking evil of him or rebelling, which brings a man into difficulties he cannot get out of; self-commendation, which is the height of folly and the fruit of pride; and carrying oneself so haughtily towards others as to provoke them to anger. Charles Ellicott puts the phrase plainly—to lay the hand on the mouth is to be silent—and says Agur is deprecating the two things that most easily lead to a quarrel, arrogance and malice, which he explains in the verse following. John Wesley reads the second clause of designing any injury against a neighbour, and the remedy as refusing to open the mouth to excuse it, repenting instead and doing so no more. Adam Clarke begins by granting the case against everybody—and who has not done foolishly at one time or other of his life?—and takes the gesture from the leper who covered his lip and cried unclean, keeping silence to all besides. His reason for the counsel is pastoral: God will blot out the offence, and neither the world nor the Church need ever know of it, for he is merciful, whereas man is rarely able to pass by a sin committed by his fellows, especially one to which he is not himself by nature inclined.

The last verse supplies the argument. Ellicott points out that one and the same Hebrew word lies behind the three English words churning, wringing and forcing, so that the sense runs as a single figure: as pressure on milk produces butter and pressure on the nose produces blood, so pressure on wrath produces strife. Gill keeps to the first term and its plain fact, that milk pressed from the udder and put into a churn yields butter when it is shaken by constant violent agitation. Clarke gives the same three clauses from the Greek version, which turns the last into a warning about speech—draw out your discourse to a great length and you may have strife and contention—and draws the practical rule from it, to avoid all strong excitements and irritations; he also quotes an older English rendering he admires for its simplicity, that whoso churneth milk maketh butter, he that rubbeth his nose maketh it bleed, and he that causeth wrath bringeth forth strife. Wesley identifies the forcing as the stirring up of wrath either in a man’s self towards others by giving way to passion, or in others by reproaches and any other provocations, and says it is the cause of many quarrels. So the chapter that opened with a man confessing he had learned no wisdom closes with the most practical wisdom of all, that the hand laid on the mouth prevents the blow.
